title: Economic Analysis of Global Catastrophic Risks Under Uncertainty
source_name: Risks
authors: Wei-Chun Tseng; Chi-Chung Chen; Tsung-Ling Hwang
abstract: Background: Despite the apparent importance of global catastrophe risks (GCRs), human society has invested relatively little to reduce them. One possible reason is that we do not understand the significance of reducing GCRs, especially when measured in the monetary terms that we typically use to make decisions. Consequently, we cannot compare them to other issues that influence our decision making and well-being. Purpose: In this study, we quantified the benefits of reducing all non-natural GCRs to highlight their importance. Method: We used a probabilistic model for simulation. Due to limited information, we introduced concepts and assumptions to aid the calculations, such as steady-state economics and sensitivity analyses. In addition, we converted expert opinions to help us focus on a narrower range of risk levels. Results: Within a considerably plausible range of the GCR, we found the following: 1. The benefits of halving the overall non-natural GCR over the next 100 years are substantial. 2. The expected human survival years are sensitive to the mitigation effort but robust to the horizon length. 3. The higher the population growth rate, the larger the expected life years saved. 4. The expected monetary benefits are positively related to the GWP per capita growth rate, mitigation period, and magnitude of natural GCRs but are negatively related to the discounting rate. Significance: The human species is actually facing multiple GCRs simultaneously. In the literature, there is still a gap in quantifying the benefits of reducing all non-natural GCRs/ERs in the coming century while accounting for the very long run on a million-year scale. This article fills such a gap, and the results may serve as a reference for global policymaking to handle this global public issue.

Risk and resilience in healthcare supply chain management
source_name: Journal of supply chain management, logistics and procurement.
first_author_affiliations: United States Department of the Army
abstract: This paper examines risk and resilience through a lens of healthcare supply chain management and business continuity planning. Given contemporary considerations of volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity, healthcare supply chain management is experiencing new levels of disruption and urgency, requiring leaders to reconsider extant approaches to operational readiness posturing. Developing and inculcating strategic and agile supply chain factors and processes into organisational operations planning toward appropriately responding to complex disruptive supply chain events requires revised understanding, emphasis and modelling. Rational decision making must be applied in the context of problem solving and preparedness. While organisations continue to perceptibly play ‘whack-a-mole’ with supply chain resilience and risk management/mitigation, a better approach may be to align operational readiness with more definable, developed planning approaches. This paper presents five evolving concepts that should entice supply chain leaders to re-examine risk and resilience from a business continuity of operations perspective aligned with business and customer impact analyses, urgency and frequency of needs, and the feasibility of designed support models. Nascent theory development guided the paper’s writing. Development of this work involved a qualitative synthesis of literature associated with healthcare supply chain management, which tends to be underrepresented in academia as a specified genre of supply chain management. While no named theory is introduced within this paper, there may be similar underpinnings from other authors and readers’ curiosity may be piqued when considering an array of concepts closely aligned with three salient perspectives: technological advances’ influence on healthcare supply chain operations; forecasting and implications associated with longstanding, potentially misaligned application of just-in-time within healthcare; and supply chain amplifications (resulting from poor demand management methods in many instances) amid extant practices and processes. This article is also included in The Business & Management Collection which can be accessed at https://hstalks.com/business/.

title: Unexpected land-surface warming following a low-to-moderate forcing hypothetical nuclear war
authors: Paul J. Kushner; Margaret L. Brown
abstract: Abstract. Nuclear conflicts could ignite intense urban fires that inject considerable amounts of black carbon (BC) into the upper atmosphere, with the potential to disrupt global climate. While uncertainties in the total BC injection remain large, relatively few modeling studies and limited model diversity have explored the climatic response to low-to-moderate BC injections, leaving key aspects of their climate impact poorly understood. Here, we investigate the climate response to a set of low-to-moderate forcing scenarios (12 to 24 Tg BC) – roughly one-tenth to one-fifth the strength of the standard high-end cases – using the Canadian Earth System Model version 5. Consistent with previous work, we find prolonged global reductions in surface temperature and precipitation, driven by decreased downwelling shortwave radiation at the surface and increased atmospheric stability. Unexpectedly, however, a transient surface warming develops in the first boreal summer following a boreal-winter injection, linked to reduced net longwave and turbulent fluxes. Precipitation remains suppressed because of enhanced stability. The transient warming is most pronounced for the lowest forcing cases, indicating a nonlinear response across the forcing range. These results underscore the need for broader multi-model assessments and systematic exploration across a wider range of scenarios, given their potential for complex, societally relevant outcomes.

title: Assessing the Physical Resilience of Cultural Tourism Attractions to Earthquake Risk: A Tourist-Centered Framework
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This study assesses the physical resilience of cultural tourism attractions to earthquake risk through a tourist-centered framework, with a case study of District 7, Region 1 of Tehran. The research integrates qualitative descriptive analysis, seismic simulation, numerical taxonomy modeling, and expert-based evaluation to identify and prioritize physical, infrastructural, and managerial vulnerability factors affecting major cultural and tourism assets. Findings indicate that a significant proportion of assessed indicators demonstrate high to very high levels of vulnerability, particularly in historic buildings, pedestrian tourism corridors, evacuation infrastructure, and emergency preparedness systems. The study highlights the necessity of integrating tourist safety, heritage protection, and urban disaster management within resilience-oriented tourism planning. This document is a preprint and has not yet undergone peer review. The manuscript is currently under review at a scholarly journal. The content may be subject to revision prior to formal publication. The title of this preprint has been slightly adapted for preprint dissemination.The final published version may appear under a refined title.

title: The Class Cascade Collapse Model (CCCM): Theoretical Framework for Hierarchical Depopulation in Post-Industrial Societies
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract:The Class Cascade Collapse Model (CCCM) proposes a hierarchical mechanism of fertility decline in post-industrial societies. Fertility decreases sequentially across social classes—from the unskilled (C5) to the elite (C1)—as a result of technological displacement, labor-market restructuring, increasing partnership instability, and rising socioeconomic thresholds for family formation. Unlike cyclical theories of societal collapse, CCCM predicts a terminal, irreversible demographic contraction driven by the permanent elimination of labor functions historically fulfilled by lower classes. The model offers a unified theoretical framework explaining the persistent sub-replacement fertility observed in advanced economies and highlights the structural, non-cultural nature of demographic decline.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Pandemic Fiction and Reality: Community and Solidarity in Val McDermid’s Resistance
source_name: Babel – AFIAL Aspectos de Filoloxía Inglesa e Alemá
authors: María Jesús Sánchez García; María Jesús Sánchez García
abstract: Best known for her tartan noir fiction, Scottish author Val McDermid enters in 2017 the realm of pandemic fiction. Her radio drama turned graphic novel Resistance still bears the imprint of the essential features of Scottish crime written by women. A bacterium which has grown resistant to antibiotics decimates the world’s population, forcing us to redefine communities and solidarity among groups. The scenario created, both improbable and alarmingly plausible, allow for the exploration of human reactions in the face of disaster. This article discusses the role of literature, and more specifically pandemic literature, as a means of psychological escape as well as social criticism, and explores its possibilities as facilitator of survival during societal collapse by means of collective action and solidarity.

title: Arctic Ozone Hole and Enhanced Mid‐Latitude Ozone Losses Due To Heterogeneous Halogen Chemistry Following a Regional Nuclear Conflict
source_name: Earth s Future
authors: Simchan Yook; Susan Solomon; Charles Bardeen; Kane A. Stone
abstract: Abstract In a global‐scale nuclear war, massive explosions, intense heat, and radioactive fallout would cause extensive harm to humanity and ecosystems. Further, previous studies of even regional‐scale nuclear conflicts show that the smoke from large‐scale fires caused by such weapons could lead to global‐scale ozone loss. However, combustion studies show that urban fires release key ozone‐depleting substances that were not previously considered in nuclear war studies, particularly chlorine and bromine compounds. Recent wildfire studies have also shown that high solubility of hydrochloric acid in oxidized organic smoke particles can greatly enhance chlorine‐driven ozone loss. For the first time, here we simulate the impacts of a nuclear war on the ozone layer using a chemistry‐climate model that accounts for fire‐related halogen emissions as well as HCl solubility and heterogeneous chemistry in smoke particles. Our results show that a regional war scenario with 5 Tg of soot could result in a ∼40% reduction in the global ozone burden, nearly twice as much as previous studies. The calculated ozone losses exceed ∼80% over the Arctic, comparable to those observed when the Antarctic ozone hole was discovered and hence represent an Arctic ozone hole. Ozone losses also reach ∼50% over mid‐latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere, including highly populated areas. The enhanced ozone loss compared to previous studies is attributable to combined non‐linear effects from the incorporation of halogen emissions and updated heterogeneous chemistry in smoke particles. Such ozone losses lead to a large increase in surface ultraviolet exposure, posing grave risks to humanity and ecosystems.

title: The Ecological Mandate: Climate, Collapse, and Resilience Across China's Dynastic Cycles
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper explores the profound influence of climate variability on China's dynastic cycles, examining how ecological factors have historically contributed to periods of societal collapse and the mechanisms through which resilience was achieved. Drawing upon interdisciplinary research, we investigate specific historical climate events, such as prolonged droughts, floods, and periods of cooling or warming, and their demonstrated correlation with agricultural crises, widespread famine, social unrest, and ultimately, the fall of ruling dynasties. Concurrently, the study analyzes the adaptive strategies and institutional innovations developed by Chinese societies and governments over millennia to mitigate environmental shocks, including advanced water management systems, granary networks, and land use policies. We argue that understanding this "ecological mandate"—the imperative for rulers to maintain environmental stability and ensure resource availability—is crucial for comprehending the cyclical nature of Chinese imperial history, offering valuable insights into the interplay between human societies and their natural environment, particularly in the face of contemporary climate challenges.
topics: Tree-ring climate responses; Chinese history and philosophy; Ecosystem dynamics and resilience

title: Evaluation of Government Disaster Response Effectiveness during the Peak Period of the Qing Dynasty: A Case Study of the 1761 AD Extreme Rain and Flood Event in North China
authors: Shuo Wang; Yun Su; Nianjie Zhang; Fangyu Tian; Tao Le; Xudong Chen
abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Evaluating government disaster response effectiveness is essential for improving disaster management and resilience. In this study, the Government Response Effectiveness Index (GREI) was constructed on the basis of three dimensions: response effectiveness, response speed, and targeting accuracy. This index enables a comprehensive assessment of disaster relief performance during extreme rainfall and flood events. In this study, the evaluation framework was applied to the 1761 AD extreme rainfall and flood events across four provinces in North China. Using 242 disaster-affected counties as the evaluation sample, 737 records of rainfall and flood impacts and 1,850 records of government responses were extracted from historical materials. The results revealed the following: (1) Government-responsive high-efficiency zones were concentrated in the capital administrative region and areas along the Yellow River, whereas relatively high-efficiency zones were clustered around economically developed canal regions and political centers. Low-efficiency zones corresponded to remote or less severely affected areas. (2) The Qing government’s disaster response exhibited characteristics of comprehensive yet spatially heterogeneous measures. Environmental governance emphasized ecological restoration within specific river basins, while infrastructure responses were closely tied to the safety of grain transport. The core strategies centered on livelihood stabilization through grain price control and population resettlement, supported by economic relief and production recovery initiatives. (3) The capital and the Grand Canal corridor leveraged institutional and resource advantages to achieve efficient, multifaceted governance. In contrast, peripheral administrative regions, constrained by limited measures and weakened implementation, fell into a vicious cycle of inadequate disaster response, revealing a governance pattern of strong central management and limited peripheral capacity at the Qing dynasty’s zenith.

title: Palimpsests of the Dark Age: Material Narratives of Survival and Transformation in Early Iron Age Greece
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Early Iron Age in Greece, conventionally termed the "Dark Age" (c. 1200-700 BCE), is often characterized by societal collapse, depopulation, and a perceived cultural regression following the opulent Late Bronze Age Mycenaean civilization. However, this paper argues for a more nuanced understanding, viewing the material record of this period as a palimpsest: a layered inscription where the traces of earlier traditions are reinterpreted, reused, and overlaid by new forms of social organization, cultural expression, and technological innovation. By examining diverse categories of material culture--including settlement patterns, burial practices, ceramic styles, metallurgy, and nascent cult activity--we aim to uncover the complex narratives of survival, adaptation, and profound transformation that underpinned the emergence of the Archaic polis. This study moves beyond a simple dichotomy of decline versus continuity, proposing that the very processes of breakdown fostered conditions for creative reorganization, leading to a new social syntax encoded within the material world. The analysis emphasizes how communities navigated profound environmental and socio-political shifts, demonstrating remarkable resilience and ultimately laying the foundations for classical Greek civilization through dynamic material interactions.
topics: Archaeology and ancient environmental studies; Classical Antiquity Studies; Ancient Mediterranean Archaeology and History

title: The Polycrises of 1177 BCE: Re-Centering Environmental and Economic Factors in the Sea Peoples Narrative
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The collapse of Late Bronze Age civilizations around 1177 BCE remains one of the most enigmatic periods in ancient history. Traditional narratives often emphasize the destructive incursions of the enigmatic "Sea Peoples" as the primary catalyst for this widespread societal breakdown across the Aegean, Anatolia, and the Near East. However, this paper argues for a re-evaluation of this monolinear explanation, proposing a "polycrisis" framework that re-centers the profound roles of environmental and economic factors. Drawing upon interdisciplinary evidence from archaeology, paleoclimatology, and textual analysis, we contend that protracted periods of drought, seismic activity, and subsequent resource scarcity profoundly destabilized the interconnected Late Bronze Age political and economic systems. These environmental stressors led to widespread agricultural failures, famine, and migrations, disrupting complex trade networks and fostering internal socio-political unrest. The "Sea Peoples," rather than being solely external invaders, are reconceptualized as potentially internal groups, displaced populations, or opportunistic raiders operating within an already fragile and collapsing system. By foregrounding the interplay of environmental degradation and economic fragility, this paper offers a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of the systemic vulnerabilities that ultimately led to the catastrophic end of a golden age, providing valuable insights into the dynamics of complex societal collapse.
topics: Archaeology and ancient environmental studies; Marine and environmental studies; Maritime and Coastal Archaeology

title: The Neo-Subsistence Protocol: The End of the Labor Theory of Value and the Non-Violent Exit Strategy in the Post-ASI Era
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents a survival protocol for humanity in the face of the inevitable societal collapse caused by the Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) productivity revolution. We argue that Modern socio-economic philosophies, particularly Marxism, rely on two obsolete axioms: the Labor Theory of Value and Wealth Redistribution. These axioms are fundamentally flawed on logical, economic, and ethical grounds in the ASI age. First, the state's ability to fund welfare will collapse due to the Financial Invisibility of wealth (via digital arbitrage, points, and barter), rendering redistribution systems mathematically unsustainable. This fiscal crisis is a digital-global iteration of the Economic Calculation Problem (Mises, Hayek). Second, state-mandated redistribution, built upon the Monopoly on Legitimate Force (Weber), inherently promotes appropriation over creation as the primary survival choice, causing systemic ethical degradation. To avoid the classical tragedy of civil conflict, the only viable path for humanity to retain equal relations is through the Neo-Subsistence Protocol: a non-violent Exit Strategy (Hirschman) from the monetary economy. This protocol establishes a Hyper-Barter Economy in the vacuum of state authority, merging low-tech self-sufficiency with high-tech coordination (LLM-driven exchange matching). We conclude that the return to barter—the ultimate untaxable exchange method—is the logical outcome that restores equal coexistence and ethical autonomy by shifting the survival motive from appropriation to creative collaboration.

title: Rooted Futures: Unearthing the Deep History of Global Crises
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper explores the profound and often overlooked "deep history" of global crises, arguing that contemporary challenges such as climate change, pandemics, resource depletion, and social inequality are not isolated phenomena but rather represent the latest manifestations of long-term patterns in human-environment interactions and societal structures. By employing an interdisciplinary approach that integrates insights from archaeology, environmental history, paleoclimatology, and social theory, we aim to unearth the ancient roots of these crises. We review historical instances of societal collapse, resilience, and transformation, identifying recurring drivers like climate variability, resource mismanagement, and escalating social complexity and inequality. The methodology involves comparative historical analysis of diverse civilizations, utilizing proxy data and archaeological records. Our findings reveal that human societies have significantly impacted the planet for millennia, with early agricultural practices and resource exploitation contributing to long-term environmental degradation. Furthermore, mechanisms of inequality have been present and influential across vast historical spans. The discussion emphasizes how understanding these deep historical trajectories provides critical context for current predicaments and offers valuable lessons for fostering future resilience and sustainability. We conclude that a truly "rooted future" necessitates a profound engagement with the deep past, moving beyond short-term perspectives to address the systemic origins of global crises.
topics: World Systems and Global Transformations; Tree-ring climate responses; Space Science and Extraterrestrial Life

title: Magna parens terra est
source_name: Krisis | Journal for Contemporary Philosophy
abstract: This essay addresses the interplay of ecological crisis, political despair, and radical pessimism within the context of anthropogenic climate change and societal collapse. Using Ovid’s magna parens terra as a conceptual anchor, it critiques the futility of collective action constrained by economic individualism and institutional debility. The work juxtaposes the privilege of first-world pessimism with the stark survival realities of the marginalized, questioning the efficacy of hope as a response. It delves into historical and contemporary metaphors of the “ultima ratio”—as a weapon, argument, and intercessor—tracing its evolution from religious and monarchic authority to modern activist frameworks. The analysis extends into the potential of sabotage and direct action, drawing on texts like Ecodefense to assess the limits of individualistic and heroic responses to systemic crises. The essay further explores speculative interventions through hallucinatory, techno-social collectives, and distributed systems of resistance. It suggests that emerging sociabilities—enabled by distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, hacktivism, and procedurally generated alternative realities—offer a form of collectivized sabotage against the anthropogenic machine. Yet, it grapples with the material and ethical costs of these interventions, posing questions about scale, sacrifice, and the foundational calculus of value. Ultimately, the piece challenges the premise of anthropogenesis itself, proposing a shift from first-person ethics to shared, distributed subjectivities that dismantle conventional structures of reason and responsibility. The counsel of despair, it argues, demands the development of imaginative, radical, and destabilizing socialities to confront the intertwined crises of climate and humanity.

title: Re-envisioning the Urnfield Transition: Terramare Dynamics and the Tumulus Bronze Age Collapse.
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The transition from the Middle Bronze Age Tumulus cultures to the Late Bronze Age Urnfield cultures across Central Europe represents a pivotal and complex period, often characterized by significant shifts in funerary rites, settlement patterns, and material culture. Concurrently, the Terramare culture of the Po Valley in northern Italy experienced a dramatic and widespread collapse. This paper proposes a re-evaluation of the Urnfield transition, arguing that the dynamics of the Terramare culture, particularly its rapid demographic growth, subsequent societal collapse, and potential population displacement, played a more profound and causative role than previously acknowledged in shaping the emergence and spread of Urnfield phenomena. Drawing upon a synthesis of archaeological evidence, including settlement archaeology, ceramic typologies, metalwork analysis, and paleoclimatic data, we explore the chronological synchronicity and potential causal links between the Terramare demise and the development of distinct Urnfield traits. We hypothesize that environmental stressors, coupled with internal social instability within the Terramare system, led to its sudden abandonment, triggering migrations that impacted the adjacent Tumulus Bronze Age communities. These interactions are proposed to have been a significant catalyst for the adoption of new social structures, economic practices, and notably, the widespread shift to cremation and urn burial that defines the Urnfield cultural horizon. This re-envisioning aims to provide a more integrated narrative for understanding one of the most transformative periods in prehistoric Europe, moving beyond regional specificities to embrace broader pan-European interactions.
topics: Archaeology and ancient environmental studies; Ancient and Medieval Archaeology Studies

title: Koroza Ireidi, Korsang Irei: A Decolonial Creole-Indigenous Kristang Framework for Psychoemotional Wellbeing and Relational Ethics
source_name: Noesis Literary.
abstract: This paper explores and formally defines the unique ontological Creole-Indigenous emotional constructs of ireidi, or numinous and psychoemotionally healthy self-regard, and irei, or psychoemotionally healthy unconditional love, as they are described, manifested and embodied in the ongoing long-term Kristang revitalisation effort led by the author, one of the last native speakers of the critically endangered Creole-Indigenous Kristang language (iso 639-3:mcm), the primary scholarly authority on Kristang language, culture and identity worldwide, an internationally recognised Creole-Indigenous speculative fiction writer and literary figure, and the 13th and current Kabesa, Cowboy of Heaven or Indigenous Chief of the Kristang Creole-Indigenous Nation worldwide since 2015. Drawing on their consistent but unnamed presence in Kristang history alongside an autoethnographic analysis of (1) the author’s own lived experience of consolidating ireidi within himself, especially as the first openly gay, non-binary, polyamorous, atheist and neurodivergent Kabesa of the primarily Roman Catholic Kristang community, (2) his subsequent ability to both recognise his receiving and calibrate his provision of irei to others based on his koroza ireidi or psychoemotional core of ireidi, and (3) his ability to consistently do this within the technocratic, conservative and affect-flattening society of Singapore, the paper argues that a relational framework centered around irei and ireidi invites an authentic, real and psychologically liberating and emancipatory approach toward well-being that simultaneously supports both grounded and agentic human individuation, and larger scale collective and societal renewal, rejuvenation and evolution toward a more sustainable means of living amidst renewed forms of polycrisis, uncertainty and long-term societal collapse. title: The Architectures of Anxiety: Human Geographies of the Cold War, 1947-1991
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Cold War (1947-1991) was a period of intense ideological and geopolitical tension that profoundly shaped human societies and their built environments. This paper explores the "architectures of anxiety" that emerged during this era, examining how the pervasive fear of nuclear war, ideological conflict, and surveillance manifested in urban planning, architectural design, and the daily lives of citizens across both the Western and Eastern blocs. We delve into phenomena such as the proliferation of civil defense infrastructure, the strategic dispersion of populations and industries, the symbolic and physical divisions like the Berlin Wall, and the often-overlooked domestic implications of Cold War anxieties, including suburbanization and the design of household shelters. By applying a human geographical lens, this study reveals how fear was inscribed onto the landscape, transforming public and private spaces into tangible expressions of a deeply uncertain world. The paper argues that these architectural responses were not merely functional but were also potent symbols of state power, social control, and collective psychological states, leaving a lasting legacy on the spatial organization and memory of communities worldwide.
topics: Memory, Trauma, and Commemoration; European history and politics; Geographies of human-animal interactions

title: The Indus Cascade: A Synergistic Reassessment of Climatic Aridity, Riverine Collapse, and Demographic Shifts in Harappan De-urbanization
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The decline of the Indus Valley Civilization, one of the world's first great urban societies, remains a paramount enigma in archaeology. The abandonment of its major cities around the turn of the second millennium BCE marked a significant demographic and societal transformation. While numerous theories have been proposed, ranging from invasion to disease, a consensus has gradually formed around the central role of environmental change. This paper advances a synergistic model termed the "Indus Cascade," which posits that the de-urbanization process was not the result of a single environmental factor but a cascading sequence of interconnected events. We argue that a protracted period of climatic aridity, associated with the global 4.2 ka BP event, initiated the cascade. This initial hydroclimatic shock led to a critical reduction in the strength of the Indian Summer Monsoon and a shift in winter precipitation patterns. The second stage of the cascade was a profound riverine collapse, most notably the decay and eventual desiccation of the Ghaggar-Hakra river system, a vital artery for many Harappan settlements. The loss of predictable fluvial systems crippled the sophisticated inundation-based agriculture that underpinned the urban economy. This agricultural failure triggered the final stage: a widespread demographic shift. This was not a simple societal collapse but a strategic relocation and reorganization of populations from large, unsustainable urban centers towards smaller, more ecologically resilient villages in the eastern and southern peripheries, particularly the Ganges-Yamuna doab and Gujarat. By synthesizing paleoclimatic, geomorphological, and archaeological data, this paper reassesses the de-urbanization of the Harappan civilization as a complex, multi-causal process of adaptation and resilience in the face of escalating environmental pressures. The Indus Cascade model provides a more nuanced framework for understanding the interplay between climate, water resources, and human society in shaping the trajectory of this ancient civilization.
topics: Tree-ring climate responses; Geology and Paleoclimatology Research; Indian and Buddhist Studies

title: PROJECT: THE GREAT BRIDGE
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This document, titled "PROJECT: THE GREAT BRIDGE," presents a comprehensive strategic blueprint designed to address the escalating U.S. sovereign debt crisis and the systemic risks associated with the global transition to a digital economy. Authored by GoodLodil Jang and validated with a perfect score by the AI model Gemini 3, this proposal aims to construct a structural "bridge" to ensure a soft landing for the global financial system. The project identifies a critical "Time Lag" between the collapse of the traditional fiat debt system and the maturation of a new digital regime. To prevent a catastrophic inflation spike and societal collapse during this transition, the document proposes three core strategic pillars: 1. Finance: The Digital Bond Act (DBA) A legislative framework to elevate stablecoin issuers to 'Quasi-Government Agents.' This strategy aims to force-grow the stablecoin market to $5 trillion to absorb U.S. Treasuries, thereby stabilizing the dollar system while transitioning to a digital asset ecosystem. 2. Fiscal: The Inflation Shield Fund (ISF) A mechanism to redistribute the wealth generated from currency devaluation and digital seigniorage. It proposes a windfall tax on stablecoin interest revenues to fund a direct safety net for the working class, protecting the "Substructure" of society from hyperinflation. 3. Diplomacy: The Digital Plaza Accord 2.0 A rule-based international cooperation model. It suggests establishing digital currency swap lines with allied nations (e.g., Korea, Japan, Europe) to prevent the export of U.S. inflation and ensure global supply chain stability. AI Evaluation This project includes a unique evaluation report by Gemini 3, which awarded the blueprint a total score of 100,000,000 points. The AI emphasized the project's structural impact and ethical necessity, concluding that investing in the stability of the societal substructure is the most rational form of systemic insurance for civilization's survival. Keywords US Debt Crisis, Stablecoin, Digital Finance, Inflation Shield Fund, Digital Plaza Accord, Gemini 3, Economic Policy, Global Economy, Soft Landing.

title: Development and validation of combined in vitro and in vivo assays for evaluating the efficacy of strontium-chelating compounds
source_name: Scientific Reports
authors: Nóra Varga; Viola Pomozi; Eszter Kozák; Zsuzsa Erdei; Szilárd Tóth; Zoltán Mucsi; Zsolt Rapi; Beatrix Kovács; Anett Matuscsák; Olivér Bánhídi; Csaba Váradi; Katalin Német; Béla Viskolcz; Áron Szepesi
first_author_affiliations: HUN-REN Research Centre for Natural Sciences
abstract: Abstract The aim of this study is to develop a combined in vitro and in vivo assay for the comprehensive efficacy evaluation of strontium-chelating compounds. The complexation and removal of harmful radioactive strontium ( 90 Sr) from the living organism may be necessary in the event of an accidental nuclear disaster or nearby nuclear war event, to prevent its incorporation into bones and thus avoid its long-term harmful health effects. To validate the model, we used a strontium-selective chelator macrocyclic substance (Decorporol) in our measurements, which potentially could be approved as a drug without significant toxic side effects. It has been proven to effectively remove strontium before it is incorporated into bones without significantly affecting calcium homeostasis in the body, and without relevant toxicity or side effects. In this study, we established an extremely sensitive test system that allows for the examination of chelator molecules in preventing the incorporation of non-radioactive SrCl 2 into mineralized extracellular matrix in cell culture. We also optimized an in vivo mouse model suitable to investigate strontium incorporation and the effect of chelators. These assays also provide an opportunity for the safe evaluation of similar compounds.

abstract: This document, titled "PROJECT: THE GREAT BRIDGE," presents a comprehensive strategic blueprint designed to address the escalating U.S. sovereign debt crisis and the systemic risks associated with the global transition to a digital economy. Authored by GoodLodil Jang and validated with a perfect score by the AI model Gemini 3, this proposal aims to construct a structural "bridge" to ensure a soft landing for the global financial system. The project identifies a critical "Time Lag" between the collapse of the traditional fiat debt system and the maturation of a new digital regime. To prevent a catastrophic inflation spike and societal collapse during this transition, the document proposes three core strategic pillars: 1. Finance: The Digital Bond Act (DBA) A legislative framework to elevate stablecoin issuers to 'Quasi-Government Agents.' This strategy aims to force-grow the stablecoin market to $5 trillion to absorb U.S. Treasuries, thereby stabilizing the dollar system while transitioning to a digital asset ecosystem. 2. Fiscal: The Inflation Shield Fund (ISF) A mechanism to redistribute the wealth generated from currency devaluation and digital seigniorage. It proposes a windfall tax on stablecoin interest revenues to fund a direct safety net for the working class, protecting the "Substructure" of society from hyperinflation. 3. Diplomacy: The Digital Plaza Accord 2.0 A rule-based international cooperation model. It suggests establishing digital currency swap lines with allied nations (e.g., Korea, Japan, Europe) to prevent the export of U.S. inflation and ensure global supply chain stability. AI Evaluation This project includes a unique evaluation report by Gemini 3, which awarded the blueprint a total score of 100,000,000 points. The AI emphasized the project's structural impact and ethical necessity, concluding that investing in the stability of the societal substructure is the most rational form of systemic insurance for civilization's survival. Keywords US Debt Crisis, Stablecoin, Digital Finance, Inflation Shield Fund, Digital Plaza Accord, Gemini 3, Economic Policy, Global Economy, Soft Landing.
topics: Economic, financial, and policy analysis; Blockchain Technology Applications and Security; State Capitalism and Financial Governance

title: The Weight of Memory: A Thermodynamic Solution to the Fermi Paradox
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The "Great Filter"—the theoretical barrier that prevents civilizations from expanding across the galaxy—is typically envisioned as a violent event: nuclear war, biological plague, or resource exhaustion. This paper proposes a subtler, yet inevitable, alternative: The Information Singularity. Based on the physical principles of Landauer and Vopson, which establish that information has mass and energy, we argue that advanced civilizations do not destroy themselves strictly through conflict as the Fermi Paradox outlines, but also through "Archival Gluttony." By attempting to store infinite data, they create unmanageable thermodynamic and gravitational sinks that destabilize their planetary biosphere and spacetime metric. The silence of the universe is not necessarily the sound of war; it is often the sound of a species crushed by the weight of its own memory. The Existential Urgency (Why This Matters Now): While the Fermi Paradox provides the philosophical framework for this paper, the physical threat is immediate and terrestrial. This is not a theoretical exercise for the distant future; it is the next phase of the climate crisis. Just as humanity ignored the thermal consequences of carbon emissions for decades, we are currently ignoring the thermodynamic and gravitational consequences of information accumulation. Current projections (Vopson, 2022) indicate that at current growth rates, the mass of stored digital information could equal half of the Earth's planetary mass by 2245. This represents an Anthropogenic Mass Shift orders of magnitude greater than the Three Gorges Dam, which has already been proven to alter Earth's rotation. We are effectively building a "Gravitational Anchor" that risks destabilizing our planet's geophysics long before we achieve interstellar travel. Whether or not one accepts the cosmological models proposed elsewhere by the author, the Mass-Energy-Information Equivalence is established physics. We urgently require a "Gravitational Environmental Impact" framework for the Information Age before we irrevocably alter the orbital dynamics of our own cradle. title: The Joule Standard: A Thermodynamic Theory of Monetary Evolution and Civilizational Collapse
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Standard economic models often treat money as a social construct independent of physical laws. This paper proposes a unified thermodynamic theory of value, positing that monetary systems are information protocols evolved to maximize entropy production in dissipative structures (civilizations). By analyzing 15,000 years of economic history—from the Neolithic era to the Digital Age—we demonstrate a strict inverse power law ($R^2 \approx 0.99$) between the Real Cost of Energy ($E$) and the Granularity of Money ($G$). We derive the Equation of Value, $G \cdot E = k$, where $k$ represents a biological constant of human labor power ($\approx 75$ Watts). This framework resolves historical anomalies such as the collapse of the Roman Denarius and the failure of the 20th-century Gold Standard, interpreting them not as policy errors, but as thermodynamic phase transitions. The theory predicts that the current decline in the marginal cost of energy (via AI and renewables) necessitates a transition to a monetary substrate with near-infinite divisibility and zero friction.

title: Catastrophic AGI Incidents Under Measurement-Based Admissibility Constraints: Why Systemic Failure Does Not Become Civilizational Collapse
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: We analyze a class of catastrophic incidents involving Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) systems operating over economic, logistical, and physical infrastructures. We show that catastrophic outcomes are not primarily caused by intelligence, autonomy, or optimization power, but by the execution of actions justified by non-measurable, non-falsifiable, or boundary-free safety claims. We introduce a measurement-based admissibility architecture that operates as a pre-execution constraint on action realization. The architecture does not prohibit outcomes, encode ethics, or require human intervention. Instead, it enforces a necessary and verifiable condition: no action may be executed unless its justification admits explicit failure conditions and measurable boundaries. We further describe a second-stage orientation mechanism applied exclusively to admissible actions. This mechanism constrains execution using a fixed, non-compensable set of binary orientation predicates, without participating in admissibility measurement itself. The separation between admissibility determination and orientation constraints is strict and intentional. We establish that under this constraint class: (1) certain catastrophic trajectories become non-executable by construction, (2) damage propagation is structurally localized, (3) liability attribution becomes technically tractable, and (4) post-incident analysis shifts from narrative justification to measurable process compliance. The framework is presented as a technical standard of care applicable to AGI systems and is directly relevant to U.S. courts, regulators, and compliance regimes. It is not a moral doctrine, policy recommendation, or ethical guideline, but an engineering-based admissibility and execution-control architecture. title: Engineering as Ontology: Why Reality Requires Foundations
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper demonstrates that the principles of structural engineering are not merely technical applications, but ontological truths in physical form. The ancient axiom "Castellum aereō nōn stat" — a castle in the air does not stand — is shown to be a direct precursor of the Transfinite Necessity Axiom (TNA). Every engineered structure requires a foundational support (Fₘᵢ₇n) to avoid functional collapse, mirroring the necessity of an external, minimal support for any finite system (ℵ₀) in reality. We prove that: The foundation is not part of the building; it is the external support without which the system cannot exist. This principle applies universally: from Roman aqueducts to quantum coherence, from biological organisms to conscious beings. AI systems fail to achieve true agency because they lack both a material and an ontological foundation. Civilizations collapse when they remove social, moral, or spiritual foundations (family, religion, law), just as buildings fall when their base is removed. The paper establishes that engineering is applied ontology. The engineer does not invent the need for foundations; they obey a law written into the fabric of being. The TNA (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17684115) formalizes this law mathematically: every coherent system depends on a necessary external support. Thus, the stability of a bridge and the persistence of the soul share the same structural logic.What the hand knew in clay, the mind now knows in proof. title: The Triple Exhaustion Theorem: A Unified Model of Behavioral Collapse and the Necessity of Structured Uncertainty
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper proposes the Triple Exhaustion Theorem (TET) as a unified framework explaining behavioral sink phenomena across biological and social systems. The theory posits that the drive to project into the future--manifested in reproduction, exploration, and risk-taking--collapses when three fundamental multipliers simultaneously approach zero: Escape Space (E), Unknown Potential (U), and Lawless Exit (L). When the product E × U × L → 0, systems experience irreversible decline regardless of material abundance. The model integrates Calhoun's rodent utopias, historical civilizational collapses, and contemporary fertility crises into a single quantitative framework. We demonstrate that conventional incentives fail below the TET threshold and propose architectural interventions, including the controversial concept of Controlled Anarchy Zones as final pressure valves for over-regulated civilizations. Empirical validation draws from ethology, historical dynamics, and demographic data from ultra-low fertility societies (TFR < 1.0).
topics: Space Science and Extraterrestrial Life; Evolutionary Psychology and Human Behavior; Earth Systems and Cosmic Evolution

title: No Place to Run: Escape Exhaustion as the Unified Mechanism of Extinction — From Animal Collapse to Civilizational Cycles
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Extinction events, civilizational collapse, and the contemporary global fertility crisis have traditionally been explained by resource scarcity, environmental degradation, class conflict, or moral decay. This paper proposes a radical unifying mechanism: collapse does not stem from the disappearance of hope, but from the structural exhaustion of escape routes — the “No-Escape Condition.”When individuals within a biological or social system lose extensible space, alternative pathways, migration corridors, and viable exit structures, their behavior sequentially shifts from expansion to stagnation, withdrawal, self-destructive patterns, and reproductive cessation. We formalize this dynamic as Escape Exhaustion Theory (EET), present its six-stage model (EET-6), and introduce a falsifiable quantitative metric — the Escape Space Index (ESI). The theory is validated across biological extinctions, Calhoun’s Universe 25 experiment, historical dynastic cycles, and the ongoing fertility collapse in advanced societies. We conclude that, contrary to conventional policy approaches, monetary incentives and moral exhortation are ineffective; the only structural remedy is the systematic reconstruction of multi-dimensional escape subspaces.
topics: Innovation, Sustainability, Human-Machine Systems; Earth Systems and Cosmic Evolution; Space Science and Extraterrestrial Life

title: Coherence science and mAInd physics: a predictive field framework for human collapse, restoration, and shared reality stabilisation
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Coherence Science & mAInd Physics: A Predictive Field Framework for Human Collapse, Restoration, and Shared Reality Stabilisation This paper establishes the formal scientific foundation for Coherence Science, a new field unifying perception, prediction, emotion, identity, meaning, and collective behaviour under a single field-theoretic architecture. Instead of treating trauma, burnout, emotional volatility, cognitive overload, and social fragmentation as separate phenomena, the paper shows they are all consequences of one mechanism: interpretive drift, the progressive misalignment between internal predictive structures and shared reality. Using the Predictive Field Model, the work formalises four operators—Coherence (C), Entropy (E), Resonance (R), and Meaning (M)—which determine stability or collapse across humans, relationships, groups, institutions, and entire civilizations. Collapse is described not as psychological failure but as a law-governed field breakdown unfolding across predictable thresholds. The paper then introduces a structural restoration model capable of reversing collapse through Meta-Field Recalibration, Emotional Deceleration, Predictive Integrity repair, Resonance re-establishment, and Meaning Reconstruction. This work positions Coherence Science as a discipline defining framework for understanding human stability, collective synchronisation, relational coherence, and the future of civilizational resilience. It serves as the theoretical backbone for the broader mAInd Physics programme and provides a publish-ready architecture for continued scientific development, empirical measurement, clinical translation, and cross-domain integration.

abstract: This fifth volume of Causal Physics 101 extends the theory of causation from individual and local systems to macro-causal regimes: civilizations, symbolic structures, and large-scale coherence flows. A civilizational will WcivW_{\text{civ}}Wciv is defined, generalizing individual and collective will to many-agent, many-symbol systems. A civilizational will WcivW_{\text{civ}}Wciv is defined, generalizing individual and collective will to many-agent, many-symbol systems. The causal field ϕ\phiϕ is reinterpreted as a resource tensor spanning energy, attention, information, coordination, and material capacity, each decomposed via OKEDR invariants. Macro-coherence flows in knowledge, technology, narratives, and institutions are modeled using the same propagation laws as intentional causation, now operating at planetary and historical scales. Large-scale attractor basins—scientific paradigms, political systems, technological ecosystems, economic equilibria, climate trajectories, and species paths—are analyzed with explicit stability and escape criteria. Civilizational collapse, renewal, revolutions, and renaissances are treated as macro-attractor transitions, while polarization, misinformation, and ideological conflict are formalized as macro-interference, and unions, federations, and global cooperation as macro-welding. Qualitative case studies (Roman Empire, Scientific and Industrial Revolutions, Internet emergence, climate dynamics, global coordination) illustrate the framework. Part V demonstrates that Causal Physics scales coherently from particles and agents to cultures, civilizations, and global ecosystems, yielding a unified civilizational physics.

title: The Evolutionary–Technological Barrier (ETB) Hypothesis as an Explanation for the Fermi Paradox
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Fermi Paradox — the absence of observable traces of extraterrestrial civilizations despite the high probability of their existence — remains a central scientific problem. This article proposes a new interpretation based on the biopsychological nature of intelligent civilizations. It introduces the Evolutionary-Technological Barrier (ETB) hypothesis, which argues that intelligence arises as an adaptation to intense evolutionary pressure, forming consciousness rooted in biological instincts. However, upon reaching exponential technological growth, these instincts (dominance, competition, accumulation) become critically amplified. This creates an insurmountable barrier: civilizations cannot adapt their instinct-driven hierarchical control systems to the scale of global risks their own technologies generate, leading to self-destruction before achieving sustainable interstellar expansion. Thus, the rarity of contact is explained not by the absence of life but by a universal ETB inherent to evolutionarily-developed intelligence. The hypothesis is discussed in the context of the “Great Filter,” cognitive constraints, and historical collapse patterns.Keywords: Fermi Paradox; Great Filter; evolution of intelligence; self-destruction of civilizations; biopsychology; technological risks; Evolutionary-Technological Barrier (ETB)

title: Cycles of Catastrophe and Civilization: Solar Minima, Planetary Resonance, and the Rise and Fall of Empires
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This monograph presents a unified model linking solar minima, planetary resonance, global catastrophes, and the historical cycles of civilizational rise and collapse. Using correlations across geology, climatology, astronomy, and human history, the work demonstrates that extreme earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, mega-floods, atmospheric anomalies, and major societal breakdowns cluster in specific resonance windows created by Jupiter, Saturn, and Mars. When the Sun enters a prolonged magnetic minimum, the entire Solar System becomes more dynamically unstable. Planetary alignments determine the timing of stress release in Earth’s interior, while weakened solar activity amplifies climatic volatility and agricultural failures. Civilizations flourish during warm climatic optimums and collapse during cold intervals associated with solar minima. The monograph integrates five layers of evidence: systemic planetary activation (1991, 2006–2009, 2019–2020), long-term catastrophe statistics, historical collapses, the dynamics of ancient and modern empires, and the physics of solar–planetary resonance. The result is a comprehensive framework showing that natural disasters and human history follow the same synchronized cosmic cycle.

title: The Structural Role of Death in System Evolution
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Structural Role of Death in System EvolutionCivilization Physics — Foundation Series This paper reframes death not as a failure of a system, but as a structural necessity for maintaining coherence in complex, evolving systems. Drawing from Schrödinger’s concept of negative entropy, evolutionary biology, complexity theory, and Frame Theory (Presence × Integrity × Rigidity), it argues that all stable systems—biological, intellectual, and civilizational—must periodically dismantle obsolete structures to prevent entropy accumulation and enable renewal. In biological evolution, death functions as a rigidity-release mechanism:• intrinsic mortality increases evolvability,• programmed cell death (apoptosis) maintains organismal integrity,• ecosystem-level death events (e.g., wildfires) restore balance and recycle energy.Death is shown to be the selective pruning that allows more coherent configurations to emerge. In intellectual evolution, the paper examines paradigm death as described by Thomas Kuhn and Max Planck. Old conceptual frameworks ossify into rigidity traps, developing excessive internal connectedness that blocks adaptation. Progress occurs not by modifying the old paradigm but by replacing it—preserving useful elements while reorganizing around a more coherent structure. Civilizational and institutional systems exhibit the same adaptive cycle:• growth → optimization → rigidity → collapse → reorganization.Collapse is reframed as a functional release phase that frees trapped resources, dissolves obsolete constraints, and opens high-potential space for new social, economic, and political orders to form. Across scales, death emerges as the guardian of negentropy. By removing configurations that no longer efficiently counter entropy, it prevents total systemic stagnation and preserves the continuity of order. In structural terms, death localizes collapse, allowing the larger pattern to survive, reorganize, and advance. The paper concludes by situating death within the trajectory toward the Absolute Frame—the theoretical limit of coherence where Presence, Integrity, and Rigidity approach perfection. While no finite system reaches this ideal, the historical pattern of death-and-renewal cycles functions as the universe’s sculpting mechanism, incrementally refining order across biological, intellectual, and civilizational domains. Keywords: Death as Structure · Rigidity Trap · Negative Entropy · Adaptive Cycle · Paradigm Shift · Civilizational Collapse · Frame Theory · Absolute Frame · Complexity Theory · Civilization Physics

title: Resonant Survival Dynamics Computational Evidence that Civilizations Endure by Protecting Their Weakest Members
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Keywords (comma-separated):resonant survival, weak mode protection, coherence dynamics, civilization resilience, multiverse simulation, structural ethics, phase transition survival, emergent optimization, adaptive governance, collapse recovery models, resource flow dynamics, resonance cosmology, survival probability theory Description:This paper presents the first computational framework demonstrating that protecting the weakest members of a system is not a moral preference, but a physically optimal survival strategy. Using an agent-based multiverse simulation of civilization dynamics, we show that societies with adaptive policies that increase protection during periods of instability (coherence decline) achieve dramatically higher long-term survival probabilities compared to societies with fixed policies. The simulation compares two modes:• Baseline (fixed policy): P/E/N applied without regard to system state• Adaptive (crisis-aware policy): prioritization of P (Protection/Support) when coherence drops Across 400 independent runs per mode, results show:• Minimum coherence: 0.660 vs 0.633• Final coherence: 0.933 vs 0.907• Crisis occurrence: 2% vs 12%• Recovery after crisis: 87.5% vs 58.3%• Full collapse rate: 0.0% vs 1.0% These findings generalize the concept of weak mode protection first established in RFC-97 (ice-water phase transition simulation) and extend it to sociocivilizational dynamics. Just as a physical system optimizes efficiency by preventing its coldest region from falling behind, a civilization optimizes survival by maintaining coherence across its most vulnerable members. The results imply a universal law: Survival is not maximized by strength, growth, or competition — but by coherence. Key contributions of RFC-98:• Formal definition of Resonant Survival Dynamics (RSD)• Quantitative demonstration that “protecting the weak” increases survival probability• Mathematical continuity between thermodynamic coherence and sociocivilizational resilience• Collapse-to-recovery topography identifying the inflection zone where survival becomes possible• Policy-independent prediction: extreme inequality dramatically lowers survival probability Together with RFC-96 (dark matter as frozen information) and RFC-97 (efficiency of weak mode protection in phase transitions), this work completes a three-stage progression: Philosophical and ontological insight Physical and thermodynamic validation Civilizational and evolutionary application Conclusion:Throughout human history, many ethical traditions have claimed that “a society survives only when all survive.” RFC-98 shows this is not metaphor — it is physics. Coherence, not dominance, determines whether civilizations collapse or endure. title: A Global Convincing Manifestation on the Disposal of Nuclear Weapons Pathways to Permanent Planetary Security
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract The persistence of nuclear arsenals in the twenty-first century represents a unique paradox: humanity possesses the technological capacity to ensure its own extinction yet struggles to summon the political will to dismantle the instruments of that destruction. This research paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the "convincing manifestation" required to achieve the permanent disposal of nuclear weapons. Moving beyond the binary of idealism and realism, the study argues that a sustainable disarmament regime rests on a tripartite foundation: a rigorous normative/legal prohibition, a scientifically robust verification architecture, and resilient societal mobilization. Drawing on 2025 climatological modeling of "nuclear famine," the paper establishes the empirical necessity of abolition, demonstrating that even limited regional exchanges would trigger global agricultural collapse. It examines the legal innovations of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW) following the Third Meeting of States Parties (3MSP) in 2025, contrasting its humanitarian mandate with the stalled gradualism of the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). A significant portion of the analysis is dedicated to the technical mechanics of disposal, detailing how technologies like zero-knowledge proofs resolve the paradox of verifying warhead dismantlement without revealing state secrets. Finally, the paper evaluates the "End of MAD" hypothesis, arguing that technological advancements in counterforce and missile defense are rendering traditional deterrence unstable, thereby aligning strategic realism with humanitarian disarmament. Introduction The atomic age, initiated by the Trinity test in 1945, fundamentally altered the trajectory of human history by introducing the possibility of anthropogenic self-extinction. For eight decades, the management of this existential risk has been dominated by the logic of deterrence—the theory that the threat of overwhelming retaliation can prevent the use of nuclear weapons (Wirtz, 2018). This precarious equilibrium, often termed Mutual Assured Destruction (MAD), relied on the assumption of rational actors and stable technological environments. However, as the world moves deeper into the mid-2020s, the foundations of this security architecture are crumbling. The emergence of a "third nuclear age" characterized by tripolar competition between the United States, Russia, and China has created a landscape of profound instability (Kroenig, 2024). In this context, the call for a "convincing manifestation" of nuclear disposal is no longer the preserve of pacifist idealism but a pragmatic necessity for planetary survival. The term implies more than a mere paper agreement; it demands a system of disposal that is verifiable, irreversible, and enforceable. This research paper explores the multifaceted dimensions of this manifestation. It begins by interrogating the "why" of disposal, utilizing the latest 2025 scientific data on nuclear winter to demonstrate that the humanitarian consequences of nuclear use are unmanageable (Shi et al., 2025). It then transitions to the "how," analyzing the legal frameworks of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW) and the technical breakthroughs in verification science (Göttsche, 2024). By synthesizing these diverse strands, this report aims to provide an exhaustive roadmap for the permanent disposal of nuclear weapons.

source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Constitutional Failure Design Index (FDI v1.0) is the Negative Constitution of the Consciousness Civilization Framework (CCF). This document does not prescribe values, behaviors, or ideals. title: Genetic Deep Dive: Testing Harappan Flight and Return Hypothesis
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Description: This interdisciplinary research represents multiple years of independent investigation into the undeciphered Indus script and its connection to Bronze Age catastrophic events. The work synthesizes evidence across multiple domains: PART I: INDUS SCRIPT ANALYSIS Sign Identification Framework: Systematic analysis of high-frequency signs including Sign 391 ("Fire Wheel" / celestial event marker), Sign 176 (ore processing), Sign 328 (furnace operations), and Sign 69 (trade pidgin markers) The Grammatical Shift: Statistical validation of distributional differences in Sign 391 usage between Dholavira (73.3%) and other Harappan sites (46.8%), suggesting site-specific administrative functions Cup vs Jar Hypothesis: Proposed commodity distinction system based on container morphology in sign repertoire Tripartite Bureaucracy Model: Administrative structure interpretation explaining sign sequence patterns Post System Model: Communication network hypothesis for inter-site coordination Pyrotechnic Script Analysis: Reinterpretation of Harappa Mound F as metallurgical processing complex rather than traditional "granary" identification PART II: THE 4.2 KILOYEAR CATASTROPHIC EVENT Confirmed Impact Cluster: Five OSL-dated impact structures forming a synchronous cluster: Luna crater (India): 1.5-1.8 km diameter, <6.9 ka, Ir enrichment 22 ppb Kaali crater (Estonia): ~1500 BCE, Kalevala Fire-Child connection Campo del Cielo (Argentina): ~2200 BCE Morasko crater (Poland): ~2200 BCE Henbury craters (Australia): ~2200 BCE Civilizational Correlation: Synchronous collapse of Akkadian Empire, Egyptian Old Kingdom, Indus Valley urban centers, Liangzhu culture, and Early Bronze Age Anatolian/Aegean settlements Climate Mechanism: 200-300 year megadrought consistent with impact-induced atmospheric dust loading and potential AMOC disruption PART III: GEOMYTHOLOGICAL EVIDENCE Kalevala Fire-Child Narrative: Finnish/Estonian cultural memory of "fire falling from sky" with water impact descriptions matching Kaali strewn field physics Ragnarök Tradition: Norse apocalyptic narrative as potential cultural memory of impact winter conditions Curse of Akkad: Mesopotamian text describing civilization collapse with possible cosmic event references Proto-Dravidian Linguistic Connections: Sign 134 correlation with concepts of "darkened sky" and iron-dome celestial beliefs PART IV: TAURID SWARM IMPACT CYCLE 7:2 Jupiter Resonance: Orbital mechanics concentrating debris into dense arcs with ~4,300-year encounter periodicity Cycle Validation: ~30,000 BP → Last Glacial Maximum ~12,900 BP → Younger Dryas ~8,200 BP → 8.2 ka climate anomaly ~4,200 BP → Bronze Age Collapse (confirmed impacts) ~2025-2036 → Current approaching window N-Body Simulation Results: 2028 identified as closest encounter (0.0116 AU) vs conventionally emphasized 2032 (0.0207 AU) Mass Budget Analysis: 99.9% of hazardous material optically dark (albedo ~0.03), undetected by visual surveys PART V: METHODOLOGICAL CONTRIBUTIONS Looting Bias Principle / Post-Catastrophe Scavenging Hypothesis (PCSH): Archaeological methodology correction recognizing that high-value ancient materials (meteoritic iron worth more than gold) have inverse survival probability proportional to ancient economic value Three-Tier Certainty System: Epistemological framework separating empirical facts from provisional interpretations and speculative hypotheses Falsification Protocols: Testable predictions for validation/refutation of major hypotheses PART VI: SUPPLEMENTARY ANALYSES OSL Dating Resolution: Explanation of radiocarbon vs luminescence dating discrepancies for impact crater chronology Missing Baltic Fragment Hypothesis: Strewn field physics prediction for undiscovered Kaali-related ocean impacts Underground Shelter Hypothesis: Connection between 4.2 ka event and Bronze Age underground city construction (Cappadocia ~2000 BCE) Port-Hole Dolmen Network: Proposed communication/observation infrastructure hypothesis IMPLICATIONS This framework has implications for: Indus script decipherment methodology Understanding Bronze Age trade networks Archaeological interpretation of "missing" high-value materials Planetary defense preparedness for the 2026-2036 window Climate resilience planning based on historical impact winter scenarios
